extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, and faculty) preparing research talks and colloquia
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for preparing and delivering mathematics research talks (seminars, colloquia) that complement papers by emphasizing high-level overview, intuition, and audience engagement rather than reproducing a paper verbatim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talks should complement papers
rubrics_metrics.description: A talk should 'complement' a paper by providing 'a high-level and more informal overview.' Avoid treating a talk like a projected paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to present the paper slide-for-slide or read the paper aloud. Instead select a high-level narrative and highlights that add value beyond the written paper. The talk's goal is different from the paper's: convey intuition, main ideas, and motivation rather than full technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide high-level, informal overviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a high-level, informal overview rather than detailed formalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize big-picture context, main results, and intuitive explanations. Reserve detailed statements and dense technicalities for the paper; use the talk to make the audience understand why the results matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on interesting/important components in greater detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Select interesting or important components of the work and present those with greater detail in the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than attempting to cover everything, pick a few key examples, lemmas, or constructions to explain thoroughly. This provides substance and leaves the audience with tangible takeaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how proofs were obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain 'how' the final proofs were obtained (the thought process), not just the final polished argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal heuristic reasoning, failed attempts, or key insights that led to the proof. Showing the discovery path aids understanding and makes the talk more engaging than a purely polished presentation of the finished proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background review to aid comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Include background review that helps the audience follow the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with motivating examples and basic definitions before launching into new material. Even experts appreciate fresh perspectives on basics; this levels the audience and improves accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make talks friendly to non-experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote initial minutes to basic examples and background material so the talk is accessible to non-experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For seminars or colloquia with mixed audiences, begin with simple motivating examples and intuitive explanations. Avoid jargon-heavy openings; use concrete instances to draw in listeners who are not specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pedagogical scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Present new results by first reviewing proofs of standard theorems in a similar style, then highlight key differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build from familiar material toward the new theorem so the audience can transfer understanding. This stepwise approach (scaffolding) clarifies what is genuinely new and why the new techniques are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure talks for breadth and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Colloquia and general talks should use narrative: pose open problems, reveal mysterious phenomena, frame surprising results, build suspense, and include judicious humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of a talk as telling a story. Use rhetorical devices (questions, surprises, gradual revelation) to keep broad audiences engaged. Judicious humour and well-placed open problems help maintain interest and emphasize significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose format appropriate to content (blackboard, slides, or computer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the presentation medium that best suits your content: blackboard for flexibility, transparencies/slides for detailed information, computer slides for animations/graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackboard: flexible, nonlinear, allows the audience to refer back and follow build-up. Transparencies/slides: efficient at conveying detailed information but can obscure substance with style choices. Computer slides: useful for animations/graphics; avoid letting form overtake substance. Match medium to goals (intuition vs. dense detail vs. visualisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and manage time; handle optional material
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice to gauge pacing and move optional material to the end or to 'deleted scenes' for flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearse to ensure you can cover planned material within allotted time. Place less-essential or technical details at the end so you can omit them if time runs short, preserving the narrative and main messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be genre-aware: exploit each medium's strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: "Good" math exposition is genre-aware: it knows whether it is a paper, a talk, or a blog post and uses each medium's strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt content, level, and style to the medium—use talks for intuition and engagement, papers for formal completeness, and blogs for informal exposition. Failure to respect genre leads to less effective communication (e.g., a talk that reads like a paper).
